title: Under the Sea
strapline: Eight wavy tentacles, a whale as long as the garden — diving into a world we can only imagine.
intent: Open up a habitat no child has walked through — the deep sea runs on imagination fed by facts, and both grow here.
Build rich ocean vocabulary: tentacles, fins, gills, coral, seaweed, shipwreck — words worth diving for.
Count and compare where the sea makes it irresistible: eight octopus legs, five starfish arms, a blue whale against a tiny seahorse.
Explore floating, sinking and water itself — the sea is the best excuse the water tray ever had.
Grow early care for the ocean: real creatures live in it, and what we drop ends up there.
implementation: Set the small world in shallow water when you can — creatures that actually float, dive and drip change the play entirely.
Feed in the specific vocabulary as you play: 'the octopus wrapped a tentacle round the anchor' beats 'the leg thing grabbed it'.
Count aloud as a habit of wonder: 'eight tentacles… and how many arms has the starfish?'
Test floating and sinking with shells, corks, pebbles and boats — predict first, then drop, then talk about the surprise.
Read the sea stories the room loves, then leave the props in the tray for children to retell and remake them.
Wonder honestly about the questions you can't answer — how do fish breathe? how deep does it go? — and look things up together.
Slip a piece of 'litter' into the ocean and see who notices; let the children decide what should happen about it.
key_questions: How do you think fish breathe under the water?
What might be hiding inside the shipwreck?
Which of these will float and which will sink — and what makes you say so?
How many tentacles has the octopus — and could he carry one thing in each?
What should we do about the rubbish that's floated into our ocean?

impact.text: Children use ocean vocabulary precisely in play — tentacles, fins, gills, coral, shipwreck — and try each new word on for size.
Children count the octopus's eight tentacles and the starfish's five arms, matching one treasure to each tentacle.
Children compare sea creatures by size — the whale is the biggest thing that has ever lived, the seahorse fits on a fingertip.
Children predict and test what floats and what sinks in the ocean tray, and talk about why the pebble went straight down.
Children retell favourite sea stories with the creatures as props, arguing happily about how the ending should go.
Children invent sustained underwater narratives — divers in trouble, storms, treasure in the wreck — narrating as they go.
Children notice 'litter' in the ocean, fish it out, and talk about keeping the sea safe for the creatures who live there.
Children ask real questions about the sea — how deep is it? how do fish breathe? — make their own predictions, and want to find out.

enhancements: Blue-tinted water with real shells, pebbles and fronds of 'seaweed' (ribbon or spinach!) for a sensory seabed.
A shipwreck — a broken basket or hull-shaped block — with treasure coins to hide and dive for.
A float-or-sink testing station: corks, coins, shells, sponges, a prediction mat with two hoops.
String and tape to lay out a blue whale's true length across the garden — then walk it, nose to tail.
Ice floes (frozen plates of water) for arctic creatures, melting slowly through the session.
A rock-pool tuff tray with hidden crabs and anemones for careful, gentle finding.
A 'save our sea' provocation: a little floating litter, a net, and a decision for the children to make.

playing_exploring: Water, shells and hidden treasure invite hands in before any adult says a word.
Children explore a world they can't visit, mixing what they know with what they imagine.
active_learning: Diving for every last treasure coin in the wreck is happily persistent work.
Children run the float-or-sink test again and again, refining their guesses with each drop.
creating_thinking: Children build theories about a hidden world — where the octopus sleeps, why the whale must come up for air.
The litter provocation hands children a real problem with no scripted answer — and they solve it their way.
